margherita-pizza: Put 500 g strong white flour, 7 g fast-action yeast and 10 g salt in a large bowl and stir them together.
Pour in 325 ml lukewarm water and 2 tablespoons olive oil, then mix with a wooden spoon until a shaggy dough forms and no dry flour is left.
Tip the dough onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 10 minutes, pushing it away with the heel of your hand and folding it back, until it is smooth, springy and slightly tacky.
Put the dough in an oiled bowl, cover with a damp tea towel and leave it to rest in a warm place for 1 to 2 hours, until it has doubled in size.
While the dough rests, make the sauce: blend a 400 g tin of plum tomatoes with a crushed garlic clove, a pinch of salt and a splash of olive oil. Do not cook it; it cooks on the pizza.
Heat the oven to its highest setting, at least 250 C, with a baking steel or an upturned heavy tray inside, for a full 30 minutes so the base cooks fast.
Knock the air out of the dough, divide it into four balls and let them relax for 10 minutes under the towel, which makes them easier to stretch.
Stretch each ball by hand into a thin round about 25 cm across, leaving the edge a little thicker for the crust. Avoid a rolling pin, which squeezes out the bubbles.
Spread three tablespoons of sauce over each base, leaving the rim bare, and tear 125 g of drained mozzarella over the top.
Slide the pizza onto the hot steel and bake for 7 to 9 minutes, until the crust is puffed and charred in spots and the cheese is bubbling.
Scatter fresh basil leaves over the pizza only after it comes out of the oven, so they stay green and fragrant, then drizzle with olive oil and slice.
vegetable-samosas: For the pastry, rub 4 tablespoons of oil into 250 g plain flour with half a teaspoon of salt and a teaspoon of carom seeds until it looks like breadcrumbs.
Add about 100 ml cold water a little at a time and press it into a stiff, firm dough. It should be much firmer than bread dough.
Cover the dough and let it rest for 30 minutes at room temperature so the flour hydrates and the pastry rolls out without shrinking back.
Meanwhile boil 3 large potatoes in their skins until tender, about 20 minutes, then peel and break them into rough chunks.

Fry a teaspoon of cumin seeds in oil, add a chopped green chili, grated ginger and 100 g peas, then the potatoes, garam masala, amchur and salt, and stir for 3 minutes. Let the filling cool completely.
Divide the dough into 6 balls, roll each into an oval and cut it in half. Wet the straight edge, fold it into a cone and pinch the seam.
Fill each cone with two spoonfuls of the cool filling, wet the top edge and press it shut, pleating it slightly so it seals well.
Heat oil in a deep pan to 160 to 170 C, a medium heat. Oil that is too hot blisters the pastry and leaves it raw inside.
Lower in three or four samosas and fry slowly for 10 to 12 minutes, turning them, until they are evenly golden and crisp all over.
Drain on kitchen paper and serve warm with tamarind and mint chutney.
apple-pie: Make the pastry: rub 200 g cold diced butter into 350 g plain flour with a pinch of salt until it looks like coarse crumbs, then stir in 2 tablespoons of sugar.
Add 4 to 5 tablespoons of ice-cold water and bring it together into a dough with a knife, without kneading. Visible flecks of butter make the crust flaky.
Wrap the pastry and chill it in the fridge for at least 30 minutes, so the butter firms up again and the gluten relaxes.
Peel, core and slice 1 kg of apples, mixing tart Bramleys with a sweet eating apple, and toss them with 100 g sugar, a tablespoon of cornflour, cinnamon and a squeeze of lemon.
Heat the oven to 200 C and put a baking tray inside to heat up; the hot tray helps the bottom crust cook through.
Roll out two thirds of the pastry and line a 23 cm pie dish, letting the excess hang over the edge.
Pile in the apples, mounding them in the middle because they shrink as they cook.
Roll out the rest of the pastry for the lid, lay it over the fruit, trim, and crimp the edges together with a fork. Cut two slits in the top to let the steam out.
Brush the lid with beaten egg and sprinkle it with sugar.
Bake the pie on the hot tray for 20 minutes at 200 C, then turn the oven down to 180 C and bake for another 30 to 35 minutes, until the pastry is deep golden and juices bubble through the slits.
Leave the pie to cool for at least an hour before slicing, so the juices thicken and the filling does not run.
pancakes: Sift 200 g plain flour, a teaspoon of baking powder, a pinch of salt and a tablespoon of sugar into a bowl and make a well in the centre.
Whisk 2 eggs with 300 ml milk and 25 g melted butter, pour it into the well and whisk just until smooth. A few small lumps are fine; overmixing makes the pancakes tough.
Let the batter stand for 10 minutes while the pan heats; the baking powder starts working and the pancakes rise higher.
Heat a non-stick frying pan over a medium heat and wipe it with a little butter on kitchen paper.
Pour in a small ladle of batter and leave it alone. Wait until bubbles appear all over the surface and the edges look dry and set, about 2 minutes.
Only then slide a thin spatula fully underneath and flip the pancake in one quick movement. Flipping too early is what makes pancakes tear.
Cook the second side for about a minute, until golden, and keep the pancakes warm in a low oven while you cook the rest.
Serve stacked, with maple syrup, berries or lemon and sugar.
lasagne: Fry a chopped onion, carrot and celery stick in olive oil for 10 minutes until soft, then add 500 g beef mince and brown it well, breaking it up with a spoon.
Stir in two crushed garlic cloves, a tablespoon of tomato puree, a glass of red wine and two tins of chopped tomatoes, then simmer the ragu gently for 45 minutes until thick.
For the bechamel, melt 50 g butter, stir in 50 g flour and cook for a minute, then whisk in 600 ml warm milk a little at a time and simmer until it coats the back of a spoon. Season with nutmeg.
Spread a thin layer of ragu over the bottom of a deep baking dish and cover it with a layer of dried lasagne sheets.
Repeat the layers, ragu, then bechamel, then pasta, three times, finishing with a thick layer of bechamel. Keep the ragu thick; a runny sauce gives a watery lasagne.
Scatter 50 g grated parmesan over the top.
Bake for 40 to 45 minutes, until the top is golden and the edges are bubbling and the pasta is soft when pierced with a knife.
Let the lasagne rest for 15 minutes out of the oven before cutting it. Resting lets the layers set, so each portion holds its shape instead of sliding apart.
roast-chicken: Take a 1.6 kg chicken out of the fridge an hour before cooking so it roasts evenly, and pat the skin very dry with kitchen paper.
Push a halved lemon, a few garlic cloves and a bunch of thyme into the cavity.
Rub the skin all over with softened butter, then season generously with salt and pepper.
Put the chicken in a roasting tin on a bed of thickly sliced onions and carrots, which flavour the juices for the gravy.
Roast for 20 minutes at 220 C, then turn the oven down to 190 C and roast for another 50 to 60 minutes, basting once or twice with the juices in the tin.
Check it is cooked: the juices from the thickest part of the thigh should run clear, or a thermometer should read 75 C there.
Lift the chicken onto a board, cover it loosely with foil and let the meat rest for 15 to 20 minutes before carving. The juices settle back into the meat instead of running onto the board.
While it rests, make the gravy in the tin with a spoonful of flour and the vegetable juices, then carve and serve.
chocolate-brownies: Heat the oven to 180 C (160 C fan) and line a 20 cm square tin with baking paper.
Melt 185 g dark chocolate and 185 g butter together in a bowl set over a pan of barely simmering water, stir until smooth, then let it cool for a few minutes.
Whisk 3 eggs with 275 g caster sugar for 5 minutes until pale, thick and doubled in volume. This makes the shiny, crackly top.
Pour the chocolate mixture into the eggs and fold it in gently with a spatula.
Sift in 85 g plain flour and 40 g cocoa powder and fold again, slowly, until no streaks of flour remain. Do not beat out the air.
Stir through 100 g chopped white or milk chocolate if you like, then scrape the batter into the tin and level it.

Bake for 25 minutes. The brownies are done when the top is set and papery and a skewer pushed into the middle comes out with a few moist crumbs, not wet batter. If the tin wobbles in the middle, give it 3 more minutes.
Leave them to cool completely in the tin before cutting into squares; they firm up as they cool.
chocolate-chip-cookies: Beat 115 g soft butter with 100 g light brown sugar and 50 g caster sugar until light and creamy.
Beat in one egg and a teaspoon of vanilla extract.
Stir in 175 g plain flour, half a teaspoon of bicarbonate of soda and a pinch of salt, then fold through 150 g chocolate chips.
Cover the bowl and chill the cookie dough in the fridge for at least an hour, or up to 24 hours. Chilling firms the butter so the cookies spread less, and the flavour deepens.
Heat the oven to 180 C and line two trays with baking paper.
Roll the dough into 12 balls and space them well apart, because they spread.
Bake for 10 to 12 minutes, until the edges are golden but the middles still look slightly underdone.
Leave them on the tray for 5 minutes to firm up, then move them to a wire rack to cool.
beef-stew: Cut 1 kg of beef chuck into large chunks, pat it dry and toss it in a tablespoon of seasoned flour.
Brown the beef in batches in a hot casserole with a little oil. Crowding the pan steams the meat instead of browning it.
Lower the heat and soften two chopped onions, two carrots and two celery sticks in the same pan for 10 minutes, scraping up the brown bits.
Add a tablespoon of tomato puree, two bay leaves and some thyme, then return the beef with 500 ml of beef stock and a glass of red wine.

Bring to a gentle simmer, cover and cook on the lowest heat, or in an oven at 150 C, for 2 to 2 and a half hours, until the beef is tender enough to cut with a spoon. Keep it at a bare simmer; boiling makes the meat tough.
Add chunks of potato for the last 40 minutes.
Taste, season, and serve with crusty bread.
mushroom-risotto: Soak 15 g dried porcini in 200 ml boiling water for 20 minutes, then chop them and keep the soaking liquid.
Keep 1 litre of vegetable stock hot in a pan on a low heat next to the risotto pan, with the strained porcini liquid added.
Soften a finely chopped onion in butter and olive oil for 8 minutes, then add 250 g sliced chestnut mushrooms and the porcini and cook until golden.
Add 300 g arborio rice and stir for 2 minutes until the grains are coated and look glassy at the edges.
Pour in a glass of white wine and stir until it is absorbed.

Add the hot stock one ladle at a time, stirring often and waiting until each ladle is almost absorbed before adding the next. This takes 18 to 20 minutes; the stirring releases starch and makes it creamy.
Stop when the rice is tender with a slight bite and the risotto flows slowly when you tilt the pan.
Take the pan off the heat, beat in a knob of cold butter and 50 g grated parmesan, cover and leave for 2 minutes before serving.
sushi-rolls: Rinse 300 g sushi rice in cold water, swirling and draining it, until the water runs almost clear. This removes surface starch that would make the rice gluey.
Put the rice in a pan with 330 ml water, about 1.1 cups of water for every cup of rice, and let it soak for 30 minutes.
Bring to the boil, cover with a tight lid and simmer on the lowest heat for 12 minutes, then take off the heat and leave it covered for 10 minutes more.
Warm 4 tablespoons rice vinegar with 2 tablespoons sugar and a teaspoon of salt until dissolved.
Spread the rice in a wide bowl, sprinkle over the vinegar mixture and fold it in with a slicing motion while fanning the rice to cool it to body temperature.
Lay a sheet of nori shiny side down on a bamboo mat and spread a thin, even layer of rice over it with wet fingers, leaving a 2 cm strip bare at the far edge.
Lay strips of cucumber, avocado and raw salmon in a line across the middle.
Lift the edge of the mat and roll it away from you, pressing firmly, then wet the bare strip so the roll seals.
Slice each roll into 8 pieces with a sharp, wet knife and serve with soy sauce, pickled ginger and wasabi.
ramen: Roast 1 kg of pork bones and chicken wings at 220 C for 40 minutes until browned.
Put them in a large pot with an onion, a thumb of ginger, a head of garlic and 3 litres of cold water.
Bring to the boil, skim off the scum, then simmer the broth for at least 6 hours, topping up with water so the bones stay covered. A long simmer turns it rich and cloudy.
Strain the broth and season it with soy sauce, mirin and a little salt.
Make the eggs: boil eggs for exactly 6 and a half minutes, cool them in iced water, peel, and marinate them in soy sauce and mirin for at least 4 hours.
Slice some roast pork belly and warm it in the broth.
Cook fresh ramen noodles in a separate pan of boiling water for 2 minutes, and drain them well; cooking them in the broth makes it starchy.
Put the noodles in deep bowls, ladle over the hot broth and top with the pork, a halved egg, spring onions and nori.
strawberry-cheesecake: Crush 250 g digestive biscuits to fine crumbs and stir in 100 g melted butter.
Press the crumbs firmly into the base of a 20 cm springform tin and chill it while you make the filling.
Beat 600 g full-fat cream cheese with 100 g icing sugar and a teaspoon of vanilla until smooth, without overbeating.
In another bowl whip 300 ml double cream to soft peaks, then fold it into the cream cheese mixture.
Spoon the filling over the base and smooth the top.
Chill the cheesecake in the fridge for at least 6 hours, ideally overnight, until it is completely set. It will not slice cleanly before then.
Just before serving, run a knife around the edge, release the tin and top with halved strawberries tossed in a little sugar.
tiramisu: Make 300 ml strong coffee, stir in 2 tablespoons of coffee liqueur, and let it cool.
Whisk 3 egg yolks with 75 g caster sugar until pale and thick, then beat in 250 g mascarpone until smooth.
Whisk 300 ml double cream to soft peaks and fold it into the mascarpone mixture.
Dip the sponge fingers one at a time into the coffee for just a second each side. Soaking them longer makes the tiramisu soggy.
Lay half the dipped fingers in a dish, cover them with half the cream, then repeat with the rest.
Cover and refrigerate for at least 6 hours so it sets and the flavours blend.
Dust thickly with cocoa powder just before serving.
panna-cotta: Soak 3 sheets of gelatine in a bowl of cold water for 5 minutes until floppy. For 500 ml of cream, 3 sheets give a gentle wobble; use 4 if you want to turn them out.
Heat 500 ml double cream with 50 g sugar and a split vanilla pod until steaming, but do not let it boil.
Take the pan off the heat, squeeze the water out of the gelatine and stir it into the hot cream until it dissolves completely.
Strain into a jug and let it cool for 10 minutes, stirring now and then so the vanilla seeds do not sink.
Pour into four lightly oiled moulds and chill for at least 4 hours, until set with a gentle wobble.
To turn out, dip each mould into hot water for a few seconds, then invert it onto a plate.
Serve with a sauce of berries simmered with a little sugar.
falafel-wrap: Soak 250 g dried chickpeas in plenty of cold water overnight, at least 12 hours. Do not use tinned chickpeas, which make falafel fall apart in the oil.

Drain the chickpeas well and pulse them in a food processor with a small onion, two garlic cloves, a big handful of parsley and coriander, cumin, coriander seed and salt until finely chopped but not a paste.
Stir in half a teaspoon of baking powder and chill the mixture for 30 minutes.
Shape it into walnut-sized balls, squeezing them so they hold together.
Heat oil for deep frying to 175 C. A piece of bread should turn golden in 30 seconds.
Fry the falafel in batches for 3 to 4 minutes until deep brown and crisp, then drain on paper.
Warm flatbreads, spread them with tahini sauce, add the falafel, chopped salad and pickles, and roll them up.
hummus: Soak 200 g dried chickpeas overnight in cold water with half a teaspoon of bicarbonate of soda.
Drain, cover with fresh water and simmer for 1 to 1 and a half hours until very soft and falling apart. Overcooked chickpeas make the smoothest hummus.
Drain them, keeping some of the cooking water.
Blend the lemon juice and 2 garlic cloves first, then add 120 g tahini and blend until thick.
Add the warm chickpeas and a pinch of salt and blend for 3 to 4 minutes, adding ice-cold cooking water a spoonful at a time until it is silky and light.
Spread into a shallow bowl, swirl the top, and finish with olive oil, paprika and a few whole chickpeas.
grilled-salmon: Take the salmon fillets out of the fridge 15 minutes before cooking.
Pat the skin completely dry with kitchen paper and season both sides with salt. Moisture on the skin is what stops it crisping.
Heat a heavy frying pan or griddle over a high heat until very hot, then add a thin film of oil.
Lay the fillets in skin side down and press them flat with a spatula for the first 20 seconds so the skin does not curl.
Cook without moving them for 4 to 5 minutes, until the skin is crisp and the flesh is opaque two thirds of the way up the side.
Turn them over and cook for 1 more minute, then rest them for 2 minutes.
Serve skin side up with lemon wedges and a herb dressing.
spaghetti-carbonara: Whisk 3 egg yolks and 1 whole egg with 50 g finely grated pecorino and plenty of black pepper.
Fry 150 g diced guanciale in a dry pan until the fat runs and the edges crisp.
Cook 200 g spaghetti in salted boiling water until al dente, and keep a mug of the pasta water.
Take the guanciale pan off the heat and let it cool for a minute, then tip in the drained pasta and toss it in the fat.
Pour in the egg mixture with a splash of pasta water and toss quickly. The pan must be off the heat so the eggs thicken into a creamy sauce and do not scramble.
Add more pasta water if it looks dry, and serve at once with extra pecorino and pepper.
french-onion-soup: Melt 50 g butter with a little oil in a large heavy pan, add the onions and a pinch of salt, and stir to coat.

Cook them slowly over a low to medium heat for 45 minutes to an hour, stirring every few minutes, until they are deep brown, sticky and sweet. Do not rush this with high heat or they burn instead of caramelising.
Stir in a tablespoon of flour, then a glass of dry white wine and 1.2 litres of beef stock, and simmer for 20 minutes.
Ladle the soup into ovenproof bowls, float a toast on each and pile on grated gruyere.
Grill until the cheese is bubbling and browned.
vanilla-ice-cream: Heat 300 ml whole milk and 300 ml double cream with a split vanilla pod until just steaming.
Whisk 5 egg yolks with 120 g sugar until pale.
Pour the hot milk onto the yolks slowly, whisking all the time, then pour it back into the pan.
Stir the custard over a low heat until it thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon, about 80 C. Never let it boil, or the eggs scramble; strain it at once if it starts to curdle.
Cool the custard, then chill it for at least 4 hours or overnight.
Churn in an ice cream machine until thick, then freeze until firm.
Without a machine, freeze it in a shallow tub and beat it with a fork every 30 minutes for 3 hours to break up the ice crystals.
lemon-sorbet: Dissolve 200 g sugar in 250 ml water over a low heat, then boil for 2 minutes to make a syrup.
Stir in the zest of 2 lemons and leave the syrup to cool.
Add 200 ml fresh lemon juice and chill the mixture well.
Churn in an ice cream machine until it is a soft, snowy sorbet.
With no ice cream machine, pour it into a shallow container and freeze it, scraping and stirring with a fork every 30 minutes for about 3 hours until smooth.
Let it soften for 5 minutes before scooping.
shrimp-pad-thai: Soak 200 g flat rice noodles in warm, not boiling, water for 20 to 30 minutes, until soft but still firm in the middle. They finish cooking in the wok.
Mix the sauce: 3 tablespoons tamarind paste, 3 tablespoons fish sauce and 2 tablespoons palm sugar.
Heat a wok until smoking, add oil and stir-fry 200 g raw prawns for a minute until pink, then push them aside.
Crack in 2 eggs, scramble them lightly, then add the drained noodles and the sauce and toss for 2 minutes.
Add a handful of bean sprouts and chopped spring onions and toss for 30 seconds.
Serve with crushed peanuts, chili flakes and lime wedges.
thai-green-curry: Spoon the thick cream from the top of a tin of coconut milk into a hot wok and boil it for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring, until the oil separates.
Add 3 tablespoons of green curry paste and fry it in the coconut oil for 2 minutes, until it smells fragrant. Frying the paste is what releases its aroma.
Add 400 g sliced chicken thighs and stir until coated and no longer pink.
Pour in the rest of the coconut milk and 100 ml stock, add kaffir lime leaves, a tablespoon of fish sauce and a teaspoon of palm sugar, and simmer for 10 minutes.
Add sliced bamboo shoots and Thai aubergines and simmer for 5 minutes more.
Take off the heat and stir in a big handful of Thai basil leaves at the very end, so they wilt but stay bright.
